title: Milestone: Reasons, Evidence and Causes
objective: After this level you can connect arguments, evidence and causes into one method for checking a claim.
summary: John Snow's 1854 case against the Broad Street pump, taken apart: a cluster of deaths, a brewery that stayed healthy, and a handle removed after the outbreak was already falling.

cards.headline: Milestone: London, 1854. Cholera kills 500 people in 10 days.
cards.body: Most doctors blamed the air. Halfway to Mastery, here's one real case that uses the whole chapter: an argument, the evidence behind it and a claim about cause. The doctor John Snow suspected the water. Watch how he built his case, and where it was weaker than the legend.

cards.headline: A cluster on the map
cards.body: Doctors then thought disease spread by breathing dirty air, called miasma. Snow took the addresses of the dead and plotted the cases on a map. The deaths clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. That's a correlation, and an argument: the premise, deaths cluster around the pump; the conclusion, the pump's water is spreading the disease.

cards.headline: The brewery that stayed well
cards.body: A cluster alone could hide another cause, so the useful evidence is people near the pump who didn't drink from it. A brewery stood on Broad Street, near the pump. Of more than seventy workmen, none suffered from cholera. The brewery had its own deep well, and the men were allowed malt liquor. Same street, different water, no cholera.

cards.headline: The handle, and a caution
cards.body: Snow met the parish Board of Guardians on 7 September 1854, and the pump handle came off the next day. Legend says that ended the outbreak. But Snow himself wrote that attacks had already fallen before the handle was removed. Credit the handle alone and you'd commit Level 43's post hoc fallacy. The strong evidence was the pattern, not the timing.

cards.headline: Milestone: causes checked
learned: How to test a causal claim: would the effect still happen without the supposed cause?
Why things that rise and fall together may share a hidden cause, run backward or be coincidence.
What separates a necessary condition from a sufficient one, and why most events have several causes.
Why a number stops measuring well once people are rewarded for hitting it.

questions.prompt: By Hume's rewind test, when does something count as a cause of an effect?

options.label: When it happens just before the effect
options.rationale: That's Level 43's post hoc trap: order alone.

options.label: When removing it would remove the effect
When most people agree that it did
options.rationale: Agreement isn't a test of cause.

options.label: When it is the largest thing involved
options.rationale: Size doesn't make something a cause.

questions.explanation: If the first had not been, the second never had existed: a cause makes a difference.

questions.prompt: A new team mascot arrives, then the team wins three games. Crediting the mascot commits which fallacy?

options.label: The post hoc fallacy
The straw man fallacy
options.rationale: A straw man misrepresents someone's argument.

options.label: Reversing causation
options.rationale: Nobody claims the wins brought the mascot.

options.label: The but-for test
options.rationale: The but-for test is a check on causes, not a fallacy.

questions.explanation: After this, therefore because of this: the wins came after the mascot, and nothing more was checked.

questions.prompt: Why did the Broad Street brewery workers matter to Snow's case?

options.label: They lived far away from Broad Street
options.rationale: The brewery was on Broad Street, near the pump.

options.label: They drank other water and escaped cholera
They helped Snow draw his map
options.rationale: The map came from the addresses of the dead.

options.label: They were the first people to fall ill
options.rationale: None of them suffered from cholera.

questions.explanation: Near the pump but drinking from their own well, or malt liquor, they stayed well. The water made the difference.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't removing the pump handle prove, on its own, that the pump caused the outbreak?

options.label: The handle was put back the same day
options.rationale: Nothing says it was put back.

options.label: Nobody recorded when it was removed
options.rationale: The date is recorded: the day after 7 September 1854.

options.label: Snow wasn't in London at the time
options.rationale: Snow met the Board of Guardians himself.

options.label: Cases were already falling before it came off

questions.explanation: Snow wrote that attacks had already fallen. Crediting the handle alone would be post hoc reasoning.

questions.prompt: In Snow's argument, what role does "the deaths cluster around the pump" play?

options.label: The conclusion
options.rationale: The conclusion is that the water spreads cholera.

options.label: A question
options.rationale: It's a claim: true or false.

options.label: An unstated premise
options.rationale: It's stated outright, on the map.

options.label: A premise

questions.explanation: It's the reason offered; "the water spreads the disease" is the conclusion it supports.

questions.prompt: A runny nose and watery eyes tend to show up together. What links them?

options.label: The runny nose makes the eyes water
options.rationale: Neither causes the other.

options.label: Watery eyes make the nose run
options.rationale: That's the same mistake in reverse.

options.label: A cold causes both
Pure coincidence
options.rationale: There's a real common cause here.

questions.explanation: Neither causes the other: a cold is the third factor behind both.

questions.prompt: What does Goodhart's law predict when a number becomes a target?

options.label: It becomes more accurate than before
options.rationale: The opposite: pressure breaks the link.

options.label: It no longer changes at all
options.rationale: The number often moves a lot; it just means less.

options.label: It starts causing its own goal
options.rationale: Rewarding a number doesn't make it cause the goal.

options.label: It stops being a good measure

questions.explanation: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure: people move the number without the thing it tracked.
